jewelry.title: Phremphun. Necklace, religious beads, made of seeds from a tree. May be worn as a necklace as part of Pa-chyu costume.
Phremphun. Necklace; Religious beads made of seeds from a tree. May be worn as a necklace as part of Pa-chyu costume.

garment.title: Urgyan (Urgyani Phahibo Ngha). Headdress formed of five upright sections of painted paper, each with a representation of an ancestor, held together with cloth band which is tied at the back of the head when worn.
Bhodd. Man's traditional shirt. Made of fine, machine-woven cotton.
Bakhu. Traditional cape made of hand-woven sheep's wool. Worn mainly by men, but in the past women would also wear them.

Syaanmo. Shirt and skirt worn only by Khhlyeprin shaman. Must be made all in one day, before the sun goes down. These costumes used to be made by the shaman's mother, but now are now made by a tailor and modelled after the old example.

Ten. Headdress made of feathers from tail of golden pheasant (one bunch red male, one bunch spotted female) joined by cotton band. Bound with black hair of the wild pig. Worn around hat 1993.39. Used by Pa-chyu shaman.

Rhalen. Black red and green striped Gurkha army belt decorated with cowries (can also become powerful eyes). 12 brass bells, one for each astrological sign, attached to the bottom of the belt by long twisted strands of nettle fibre. Used by Pa-chyu shaman. Gurkha belts in themselves are status items among the Tamumai (Gurungs)

textile.title: Pro. Red, velvet shawl. Everyday item of woman's clothing, worn with knot over the left shoulder. Worn by Pa-chyu during the most dangerous part of rituals in remembrance of a powerful female Pa-chyu.

A cream coloured square cloth made of four strips of woven textile, possibly nettle, stitched together with black thread. The cloth has been woven with raised ribs along the short width of the panels; the cloth has been hemmed along two edges. Twisted piece of plant fibre found with cloth.

photo.title: Pandit conducting ceremony for Gurungs at Maidel hamlet in Mukli, cf. 116.

A pious Gurung has invited a Brahmin to perform at shrine in Maidel. Audience: nine women, one man, odd children. 2 dudhilo trees, with bells. Right of bigger tree are two standing stones. Freshly red-earth-plastered jagge in foreground.
as 116-7. When seated the Brahmin was using a loose-leaf book, but here he is reciting from memory. Ceremony ends with  ṭikās, garlands and meal of roṭis on leaf plates.
A Gurung housewife is spinning on her veranda in Maidel (a hamlet of Mukli; there are very many hamlets in the 'village').

as 116, but garlanded brahmin and others are now standing. Left of him is assistant with fly-whisk. The 40ft high bamboo is planted beside a 1 ft high rectangular mound surrounded by a six-inch deep furrow.

instruments.title: Taungi. Drum, Taungi (T-K) Paduchhyan (C-K). Hemispherical, copper body with calf or goat skin made by leather-maker.

Ngha. A: Drum and B: beater, (Gurung) NGhaanrdaan (C-K). Side frame made of wood of Chaingi tree. The wood can only be cut down on a ' good' day (determined by astrology) - all materials must be obtained on a ' good' day and the drum must be assembled on a single ' good' day. This wood is difficult to get, since it does not grow everywhere and many people do not recognize it. The strip of wood is shaped by putting it in a circular hole in the ground where it is left for fifteen days. Sidelacing made of Kre creeper or vine. Skin made of goat, ideal to have the skin of a goat which has been killed by a tiger or a leopard, but this is not always possible. Old goat skin is much better and stronger. Forked piece of wood across inside of drum used as handle. This type of drum is only made and used by shamans. This one for Pa-chyu shamans and Khhlyeprin makes similar drums but the size is a little bigger. This is an old drum, possibly made by Yarjung's grandfather. Used for some mortuary and healing rituals. ' Good' rhythms for curing rituals, ' Dead', not so good rhythms used for funerals. Only shamans understand what the different rhythms mean. Rhythms must be read. The sound is better when heated, and is usually heated in the fire. This is an old drum and it makes a very strong sound, so there is no need to heat. But new drums must be heated before playing. B) Stick made of strip of bamboo; Good

Thuhnga. Iridescent conical shell used as a horn. Always blown at the beginning of the ritual before playing the drum. There are two types of blowing, one for god and one for evil spirits (to scare them).

household.title: Rhengaa. Carrying bag part of traditional Tamu Gurung man's costume, called Rhengaa, also used by pa-chyu Shaman. Made of nettle fibre. The bag is worn around shoulders, with the pouch for carrying hanging at the back and sides.
Puchai. A: Container and B: Lid made of Daar wood turned on a hand lathe. Holds millet wine. Used by Yarjung during a ritual. Made by Chunarr (?caste group).
Ra thih. Bag. Goat skin with string, rolled and used as a container for sacred material.

Pyon. Wooden container. Made by Chunar's people and ordered by a shaman on a special day. To make the container, a piece of wood is turned on a hand lathe and cut with a special blade. Used for holding wine to give the ancestors a special drink. Interior has residue of millet wine.

Ten Phahssaa. Bag with shoulder straps made from chemical compost bag. Painted by Yarjung and used as he would use a leather bag Ten Phahssaa. Use as an outer bag for carrying goat skin bundle 1993.36 which contains ritual objects.

masks-ritual.title: Dhubara. Brass incense burner. Used for burning purifying herbs during rituals by both Pa-chyu and Khhlyaprin shamans. May also be used by someone who is praying and using herbs. ' Without herbs we are dirty' (Yarjung).

Saamon. A wand made out of a bunch of peacock feathers bound with twigs at the bottom. Used by Pa-chyu shaman during ritual. When not being held during ritual, they are stood in a bowl of millet (you cannot put them on the ground). The peacock is noted for being very beautiful and powerful. A peacock feather can be used in various ways, e.g. if worried that insects will eat a book, a bit of the feather is put with the book.
Chyha (Neme). Soul catcher staff, used by Khhlyaprin shaman.

arms.title: Shairu Choh. Arrow. Bunch of porcupine quills projecting from a metal holder. Quills will fly by themselves,. They are projected forward by a Pa-chyu shaman and the quill turns and the pointed end spears a bad spirit and brings it back. Can also be used to fight with another shaman.

other.title: Fagi. Man's traditional white kilt worn for everyday. Made of fine machine-woven cotton. Previously made of hand-woven nettle fibre.

Chhyonlen. Pair of brass cymbals of a type used by Pa-chyu and Khhlyprin shamans and lamas. Those of the Khhlyprin may be larger. In the past ancestors used two stones instead of cymbals. The cymbals are the second friend of the drum, played by the Shaman's assistant to accompany the drum. Made by case of brass makers Phahde Khhle who live in city; Good
Phahsa; Ri Saida Saimain; Ta; Thahlen; Me; Khohre; Mhachyorhim; Khohja; Karda; Sanaso.

Phahyo Khauda. Brown, spotted shell. Used for healing children's respiratory problems. These shells used to be ordered from Indian but now some business men import the shells and sell them in market. Because it is pretty some people buy it only for use as a decoration.

Chyhasun. Spirit Catcher. A bird's head (chhahkra) and beak (chyhasun) of a saras used to help 1993.42 to collect the spirits. Used by Pa-chyu shaman. The bird has to be trapped on a ' special' day. N.B. It is important that the birds 1993.44-46 are all different. Each obtained on a different ' special' day as determined by astrology.
